# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This follow-up does what the earlier documents called for. It measures the hours of work not claimed on timesheets, runs a registered mediation test, follows up for 24 months, and reports honestly on the counter arm. Its replies to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are mostly fair.

The headline arithmetic checks out. But a rough hours accounting doesn't fit the mediation result, and a change in the control group complicates the "decay" story.

## 1. What checks out

- Output per hour on timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%. On system logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- The mediation shares sum correctly: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- For the 11 continuing Halden organisations: hours 34.9 / 40.3 is a fall of 13.4%, and output 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8% per hour.
- The fall from 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets is a decline of about 22%, consistent with "about a quarter."
- The counter-office cost estimate is plausible:
  - Adding 12% more staff would bring contacts back to about baseline (0.886 × 1.12 ≈ 0.99).
  - That would raise cost per contact by about 9% if staff are roughly 70–75% of costs.
  - The report should state that assumption.

## 2. The hours accounting suggests meetings explain almost all of the gain, not 47%

A rough calculation using the report's own numbers:

| | Treated | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Total hours, baseline → 24 months | 37.9 → ~33.4 (−12%) | ~stable |
| Recurring meetings | 7.4 → 3.9 | 7.2 → 7.0 |
| Non-meeting hours | ~30.5 → ~29.5 (−3.4%) | ~+0.7% |

- Relative to control, non-meeting working time fell only about 4%.
- Output per FTE fell 3.4%.
- So output per non-meeting hour is roughly unchanged (about +0.7%).

**What this implies.** Most of the hours cut came out of meetings. Staff spent about the same time on casework as before, and produced about the same output per hour of it. On this accounting, removing meetings explains nearly all of the per-hour gain, which leaves little room for the 18% fatigue share and the 35% unexplained.

**Caveats on this calculation:**
- The control group's baseline hours aren't reported, so I assumed they matched treated offices.
- Meeting time comes from calendars, which show scheduled meetings rather than meetings actually attended.
- A statistical mediation model and an hours accounting are not the same thing.

Even so, the gap is large enough that the authors should reconcile the two.

**The system-log measure needs the same check.**
- The report says log-in time records "time staff are working on cases."
- If so, it should exclude meetings, and log hours should have fallen about 4%, not 11%.
- Either the logs capture more than casework (for example, staff logged in during meetings), or the figures conflict.
- The report should say what log-in time includes. The 8.5% headline depends on it.

## 3. The control offices' meeting audit muddies the decay finding

**Part of the "decay" may come from control improving.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and improved output per hour by 4.1%. That would raise the control average by roughly 1.2 points. It would narrow the gap between treated and control without any fading in treated offices. So the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% is partly contamination of the control group, not purely fading. The report should:
- estimate the effect excluding those two offices, or using only months up to 14;
- say this explicitly in the decay discussion and in its reply to the meta-analysis.

**The decline isn't statistically established either.** The nine-month interval (+6.9 to +18.4) and the 24-month interval (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily. The report's "consistent with some fading" is fair; it shouldn't be read as demonstrated decay.

**The control meeting figures look inconsistent.**
- If two control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control average would drop by about 0.6 hours from that alone.
- The reported control average fell only 0.2 hours (7.2 to 7.0).
- That requires the other five control offices to have *increased* meetings by about half an hour each.
- Possible, but it needs explaining.

## 4. The mediation test is weaker than "confirms"

- **Timing of registration.** It was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results and the exploratory meetings finding were known. It is a genuine confirmatory test only if it uses data collected after month 11. The "larger sample of office-months" may include the months that produced the original finding. The report should state which months enter the model.
- **The mediators weren't randomised.** Only treatment assignment was randomised, not meeting cuts or fatigue. Offices with better managers might both cut meetings and raise output. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's "confirms" is too strong. "Supports" is more accurate.
- **The intervals look narrow.** There are 14 clusters, with repeated office-months that are correlated over time. A 95% interval of 28–66% seems tight. The report should state how standard errors were computed.

## 5. The Halden subset

- **Response selection.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations contacted responded. Non-response is another layer of selection, on top of the two the report acknowledges.
- **The baseline figure may belong to a different group.** The baseline of 40.3 hours exactly matches the re-analysis's figure for all 27 time-tracking organisations. If that number is reused, the per-hour figure for these 11 organisations isn't measured against their own baseline. The report should confirm which baseline it uses.
- **One reversion doesn't fit the stated reason.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But one was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's own coding, that is discretionary deadline work, not coverage-bound. It is a genuine counterexample to the work-type split and should be reported as one.
- **"Upper bound" goes too far.** Survivorship biases the estimate upward. But with no comparison group, other changes over time could push the figure in either direction. "Likely an overestimate" is defensible; "upper bound" is not.
- **Authorship.** R. Okafor is a Halden pilot author. That's worth noting, given the earlier dispute over how Halden described its attrition.

## 6. Replies to earlier claims

**To the re-analysis: fair.** The 24-month Varden estimate meets every standard the re-analysis set: record-based output, actual (here log-measured) hours, randomisation, and two-year follow-up. A gain whose interval excludes zero does refute "entirely an artifact." This holds unless the log measure turns out to be inflated (section 2).

Two qualifications:
- **Novelty isn't fully excluded.** Staff knew their assignment. And if the gain is mostly meeting removal, it isn't a novelty effect, but it isn't a reduced-hours effect in the usual sense either.
- **The re-analysis predicted a return to baseline.** It forecast energy back at baseline around month ten (my earlier calculation suggested about month nine). The 24-month result contradicts that, fairly.

**To the meta-analysis: fair, and it confirms the earlier concern.** The four long follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they can't test whether effects decay. The counterpoint that per-hour gains declined in the one controlled long-run study should be read alongside section 3: part of that decline may come from the control group improving.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Output per FTE.** The interval of −8.0% to +1.2% can't rule out a loss of about 8%. "Mostly, not fully, offset" is fair.
- **Policy implication.** The report frames the open question as whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the per-hour gain. If section 2's accounting holds, the bigger implication concerns output per employee. Cutting meetings by about 3.5 hours *without* cutting total hours could put that time into casework, and might raise output per employee rather than merely hold it. The two control offices are weak but consistent evidence. This is the obvious next trial: a meeting-reduction arm with no change in hours.

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persisting to 24 months in case-processing;
- refutation of "entirely an artifact" and of "no sign of decay";
- the counter arm's failure;
- meetings as a substantial part of the mechanism.

**Needs reconciliation before publication:**
- the hours accounting, which implies meetings explain almost all of the gain;
- what system-log hours actually measure;
- contamination of the control group from month 15, and its effect on the apparent decay;
- whether mediation used only data collected after registration;
- the Halden baseline and the marketing-agency reversion.

Taken together, the five documents point to a narrower conclusion. In discretionary work, a shorter week appears to raise output per hour mainly by squeezing out low-value time such as meetings. It is not mainly a matter of making each working hour more intense. In coverage-bound work, it doesn't pay for itself.

I can draft a referee report or a one-page synthesis of all five documents if that would help.
